A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same MIKASA benchmark. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: v2.pdf reports original online RL, offline RL, and VLA experiments, including learning curves and success rates in Table 4 and Appendix Table 6.

after.justification: v3.pdf retains these experiments and adds baseline comparisons, dense-reward offline results, and original physical-robot experiments in Appendix N.

M1.justification: The official benchmark task mechanics, observation modes, and reward structures remain unchanged. No new proposed learning algorithm or memory architecture is introduced; additional evaluated models are baselines, while customization examples expand documentation.

E1.justification: v3 adds real-world demonstration datasets and SO-101 robot evaluations under fully observable, dynamic non-occluded, and occluded object-shuffling conditions (Appendix N). This extends v2's simulated evaluation to physical sensing and manipulation. The original 32 simulated tasks and MIKASA-Base collection are retained.

E2.justification: Table 4 adds SpatialVLA and π0 alongside the retained Octo and OpenVLA comparisons. Appendix J/Table 7 adds DMamba and GTrXL to offline comparisons on five retained tasks, and Appendix N evaluates π0.5 on physical tasks.

E3.justification: Appendix H adds dense-reward offline evaluation beyond v2's sparse-reward offline comparisons. The new physical study uses 300 demonstrations per task, 100,000 fine-tuning steps, 30 evaluation episodes per task, and separate touch and pick metrics. These are additional protocols; the retained simulation VLA budget remains 250 trajectories and 50,000 iterations.

E4.justification: v3 adds an offline reward-formulation comparison on five tasks (Appendix H). Appendix N introduces staged controls for basic manipulation, dynamic-scene robustness, and occluded recall, with per-color and touch-versus-pick analyses. These extend v2's existing observability, reward sparsity, difficulty, and action-chunking analyses.

E5.justification: v2 Appendix G describes SEM over 100 evaluation episodes; v3 Appendix I specifies three training runs, 100 episodes per run, and SEM across run-level means. This changes the general reporting description without establishing increased replication: v2 Table 6 already reported three-run SEM.

E6.justification: The original VLA rows and full offline matrix are retained, but expanded Table 4 and new Tables 6, 7, and 10 add substantial results. Physical touch success is 1.00, 0.63, and 0.10 across the three conditions. New Table 7 also reports unexplained discrepancies: RATE on InterceptMedium is 0.09±0.03 versus 0.32±0.02 in retained Table 8.

T1.justification: The POMDP formulation, policy objective, correlation-horizon definition, and mathematics within retained task descriptions are unchanged. No new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or derivations are introduced; expanded memory discussions are conceptual.

C1.justification: The abstract and four central benchmark contributions retain their meaning. The conclusion adds a stronger causal claim from physical experiments: memory, rather than embodiment or perception noise, is the primary limitation. This extends the claims without redefining the benchmark's central contribution.

C2.justification: Section 7 adds specific boundaries concerning single-episode evaluation, interference, forgetting, spurious correlations, and limited metrics, while removing the explicit compute-constraint qualification on VLA fine-tuning. Appendices B and N add explanations about isolating memory from other difficulties. Appendix J claims RATE superiority despite higher GTrXL means on RememberColor5/9 in Table 7.

D1.justification: v3 adds extensive task-parameter and horizon customization guides, explicit MIT licensing, a reproducibility statement, physical-robot setup and collection details, and real-world dataset links (Table 11). These substantially expand documentation. Some examples contain errors: the ChainOfColors guide in Code 20 instead instantiates SeqOfColors.

R1.justification: Appendix F substantially expands the earlier brief memory-mechanism survey with temporal convolutions, world models, external read/write memory, implicit action-based memory, and autostigmergy, supported by additional citations. Table 3 adds LIBERO, LoHoRavens, and Ravens. The central positioning against fragmented memory benchmarks remains.

P1.justification: v3 revises the VLA discussion, limitations, and conclusion, adds a reproducibility statement, and updates affiliations, contact information, and citation style. The main section order and most earlier narrative and task descriptions remain intact; much of the appendix expansion documents new content.

P2.justification: Figure 6 is redesigned with regrouped task axes, revised category shading, and a separate legend. Tables 3 and 4 expand, and new tables and figures display additional comparisons, customization examples, and physical experiments. The ICLR format changes typography and layout; most original plots and task illustrations are retained and renumbered.

improvement.justification: The physical-robot controls and broader baseline coverage provide useful validation absent from v2, while expanded configuration and data documentation improve the benchmark's usefulness. The net gain is limited by unexplained Table 7/Table 8 discrepancies, a RATE-superiority interpretation contradicted by reported means, erroneous customization examples, and causal claims about isolating memory that exceed what the physical controls establish.
